extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners (PR managers, communicators, counselors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on planning and programming public relations campaigns, obtaining managerial buy-in, writing scenarios, and anticipating/handling crises including establishment of information centers and coordinated action/communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pretesting must reflect program conditions and target publics
rubrics_metrics.description: When using pretest results as a guide to public relations programs, practitioners need to be as certain as possible that program conditions are similar to those that existed during the pretest and that pretest subjects are representative of the program’s target publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pretest small details (example: cultural symbol on a calendar caused problems in Saudi Arabia). Be cautious: public opinion changes over time (seasonal shifts, major events like Hurricane Katrina can change fundraising climates). A successful pretest result may fail on widespread use if conditions differ or time lag changes public concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate contribution to organizational goals to get buy-in
rubrics_metrics.description: The best way to get buy-in for the public relations plan is to demonstrate how the program will help achieve organizational goals, or in the words of some managers, “affect the bottom line.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relate PR objectives to reputation, market share, employee attraction/retention, donor/member attractiveness, autonomy, and stock price. Show how PR will manage environmental threats, enhance competitive edge, and protect reputation—management expects PR to be strategic and tied to organizational mission/operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use persuasive and technical communication skills to sell the plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must use effective writing, persuasive speaking, effective use of presentation audiovisual materials, and careful reading of those around the conference table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin selling with an effective program plan. Keep explanations short and to the point, be decisive, have conviction, and focus on the future (trusted advisors are a force for tomorrow). Eliminate personal opinion except when applying special knowledge of related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarize colleagues and document agreed programming
rubrics_metrics.description: After a program has been approved at the policy level, it becomes necessary to familiarize colleagues with what is to follow; programming agreed upon should be a matter of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Putting the plan on paper makes planning tangible for implementers, helps collaborators solicit support from their teams, and prevents key participants (including outside counselors) from being uninformed. Plan not only strategies and tactics but also implementation details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planning purpose: create or prevent events and prepare contingencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Planning is for the purpose of making something happen or preventing it from happening, for the purpose of exploiting a situation or remedying one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preventive public relations ties to long-term planning; remedial PR tends to be short duration with minimal planning time. Long-term plans should include strategies for contingencies to exploit positive events or remedy problems quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write multiple planning scenarios (2–4, ideally 3) and avoid assigning probabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing planning scenarios anticipates and describes a range of possible future states; the useful range is two to four scenarios, with three ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label scenarios by major theme or attribute rather than probability (avoid 'most likely'), to prevent planners focusing strategy on a single projected future. Scenarios help plan for events with no history and enable contingency planning across possible states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scenarios when historical forecasting is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The greater the future uncertainty, the greater the need for planning scenarios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional quantitative forecasting based on historical data may not meet PR planners’ needs when preparing for unexpected events; scenarios provide qualitative, plausible alternatives for strategy development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate crises as low-probability, high-impact events requiring swift decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: An organizational crisis is a low-probability, high-impact event that threatens the viability of the organization and is characterized by ambiguity of cause, effect, and means of resolution, as well as by a belief that decisions must be made swiftly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While specific disasters are often unpredictable, planners should assume the unexpected will occur and plan accordingly; crisis anticipation and thorough planning are prerequisites to successful crisis communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine crisis type because response depends on type and duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must determine the types of crises, because the response depends in part on the type and probable duration of a particular crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly categorization includes eight types caused by management failures or environmental forces: natural, technological, confrontation, malevolence, skewed management values, deception, management misconduct, and business/economic. Knowing type informs appropriate tactics and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize crisis timing categories: immediate, emerging, sustained
rubrics_metrics.description: Crises vary by time: (1) Immediate crises happen suddenly with little time for planning; (2) Emerging crises allow more time for research and planning but may erupt suddenly; (3) Sustained crises persist for months or years despite efforts to resolve them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate crises require pre-agreed general reaction plans and consensus among top management. Emerging crises require convincing management to act before critical stage. Sustained crises involve rumors and persistent misinformation that can cause long-term reputational harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidelines for preparing for public relations crises (identify, prioritize, plan responses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare by identifying things that can go wrong and become highly visible; assess vulnerabilities; assign priorities; draft questions, answers, and resolutions for each potential scenario; focus on what to do and what to say in the first critical hours; and develop a containment/counteraction strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What-to-do guidelines include a telephone call tree listing order to inform key decision makers. What-to-say guidelines include Q&As listing likely reporter questions and appropriate answers, and 'standby statements' with situation-specific blanks to fill in when crisis occurs. Emphasize containment and counteraction rather than mere reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis checklist: immediate operational actions and coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: In a crisis: get out the prepared crisis plan; convene the crisis management steering committee; call in experts; open lines of communication; notify top management and have them make impact projections; channel all inquiries to the designated spokesperson; ensure message consistency; set up a news center; provide information quickly; demonstrate concern and explain actions; have 24-hour staffing and stay with the story; reconvene afterward to evaluate and improve the plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational details: news center should provide background packets and interview space with good cell reception and wi-fi. All information should be logged and coordinated; reconvening allows lessons-learned and plan refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis communication prohibitions (don’ts) during and after crises
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not speculate publicly about what you do not know to be fact; do not minimize or underplay serious situations; do not let the story dribble out bit by bit; do not release information that violates privacy or blames individuals; do not say 'no comment' or make off-the-record comments without explanation; do not play favorites among media; and do not try to capitalize on media attention for self-serving promotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If information is unavailable, explain why and promise to provide it when possible. Respect reporters’ work and avoid undermining their scoops. Transparency and consistency are critical to maintain control of the narrative and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish an information center distinct from media operations
rubrics_metrics.description: A standing information center should be recognized as the place where information moves from the institution directly to an organization’s publics; it is not a media operation and should not simply be another responsibility of media relations staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where feasible, maintain separate but closely coordinated media and public information centers. Separating functions preserves effectiveness and allows tailored responses to different publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure the information center in two parts: rumor-response and coordinating agency
rubrics_metrics.description: The information center should have (1) a rumor-response telephone operation handling questions and answers, and (2) a coordinating agency that contacts staff for information, checks material with top administration for accuracy, coordinates with the media relations office, logs information, and supplies material to the response center.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The coordinating agency should have qualified spokespeople for policy and philosophical discussions; it serves as the sole source for the center, ensuring a one-voice response and controlled information flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build credibility for the information center before crises
rubrics_metrics.description: Any information or fact center must have credibility established long before any crisis; the flow of credible information must be established during routine times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the information center an accepted, continuing part of the institution so internal and external publics will use it in crises. This requires education and routine use—more than a reputation for truth, it requires sustained trust-building among stakeholders and employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action program must include corrective, socially responsible organizational change
rubrics_metrics.description: The action strategy primarily involves internal organizational change and must be socially responsible; if something done caused the problem, corrective action is necessary to eliminate the original source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: university changing registration priorities to attract freshmen; BLM changing adoption policy and ownership rules for wild horses. Actions must address root causes, not merely messaging, because actions speak louder than words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate action and communication: communicate to inform, persuade, instruct
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication strategy supports the action program by (1) informing internal and external target publics of the action; (2) persuading them to support and accept the action; and (3) instructing publics in skills needed to translate intention into action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design communication components to match action steps: identify publics (consumers, regulators, media, internal staff), craft message strategy (gather facts, assure cooperation with authorities, assure determination to solve problem), and choose media strategy (how to deliver messages). Example: Johnson & Johnson’s Tylenol response combined recalls, tamper-proof packaging, liaison with authorities, and an intensive factual message campaign.
